chunks: "EEPROM is electrically erasable programmable read-only memory.
It's non-volatile, like ROM, but you can rewrite it electrically, one byte or one small page at a time, without any special erase equipment.
Each cell is a transistor with a floating gate.
To write, a higher voltage that the chip generates internally pushes electrons through a thin oxide onto the gate by tunnelling; to erase, it pulls them off.
The stored charge shifts the transistor's threshold, which is what the read circuit senses.
It stays for decades without power, but every write wears the oxide a bit, so endurance is limited, typically a hundred thousand to a million write cycles per byte.
In practice it's a small chip, from 1 kbit up to maybe 1 Mbit, on I2C or SPI, like the common 24-series parts.
Reading is fast, but a write takes a few milliseconds, during which the chip ignores the bus, so you either wait or poll for an acknowledge.
You also have to respect page boundaries, because a page write wraps around inside the page.
I'd use it for things like calibration constants, a serial number or user settings, small amounts of data that change rarely.
For large data, I'd use flash; for data that changes constantly, FRAM or wear levelling."
